# Revisiting the Performance of Deep Learning-Based Vulnerability Detection on Realistic Datasets

- Authors: Chakraborty, Partha; Arumugam, Krishna Kanth; Alfadel, Mahmoud; Nagappan, Meiyappan; McIntosh, Shane
- Year / venue: 2024, IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering (published)
- DOI: 10.1109/tse.2024.3423712 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/tse.2024.3423712
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] To test whether deep-learning vulnerability detectors that report up to 99% recall/F1 still perform in a realistic setting where the model scans entire codebases rather than only functions from fixing commits, and to provide a dataset (Real-Vul) for such evaluation (p. 1–2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] RQ1: How do DeepWukong, LineVul, ReVeal and IVDetect perform in a realistic evaluation setting compared with the setting of the original studies? RQ2: How do they perform when also trained on a similar realistic training dataset? (p. 5).
- [A] Implicit hypothesis: prior datasets (synthetic SARD; commit-sampled Big-Vul/ReVeal with near-balanced ratio and label inconsistency) overestimate performance (p. 3).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] (1) Replication of four DL models on their original datasets with an 80/20 random split (p. 5–6); (2) evaluation of these models on the Real-Vul test set (RQ1, p. 6–7); (3) retraining on Real-Vul, imbalanced and balanced (RQ2, p. 8–9); (4) discussion analyses: project size vs FPR, cyclomatic complexity, LIME token analysis, dead-code augmentation, per-CWE-cluster and per-severity F1, and two fine-tuned LLMs (p. 9–12).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] LineVul (CodeBERT, token-based), DeepWukong (GNN on XFG slices), ReVeal (GNN on code property graphs, uses SMOTE), IVDetect (graph-based with interpretation) (p. 4–5). [V] CodeLlama (7B) and Mixtral ("7B" per the paper) fine-tuned with parameter-efficient fine-tuning on Real-Vul (p. 12).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Each model's performance on its own original dataset (Table 2) is the baseline for the realistic setting (p. 6). [V] No static-analysis tool is evaluated; authors list this as future work (p. 13).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Real-Vul built from the 10 Big-Vul projects with the most vulnerabilities (Chromium, FFmpeg, ImageMagick, Jasper, Krb5, Linux, OpenSSL, php-src, QEMU, tcpdump), covering 73% of Big-Vul's vulnerable samples (p. 3–4, Table 1).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] Function. 5,528 vulnerable functions (4,418 train, 1,110 test) (p. 4); 1,682,713 uncertain functions (769,464 train, 913,249 test) (p. 4). Table 1 project sizes sum to 270,919 functions and p. 13 states "270,919 samples, of which 5,528 are vulnerable" (p. 4, p. 13).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Vulnerable functions ordered by fix date; first 80% to train, last 20% to test. Uncertain functions = all functions in a repository snapshot taken after the last training fix date (train) and after the test period (test) whose MD5 hash matches no vulnerable function, avoiding label inconsistency (p. 4). [V] Authors found 15% of vulnerable samples in ReVeal also listed as uncertain (p. 3).
- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Real-Vul and scripts released at https://zenodo.org/record/8206635 (p. 2).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] DeepWukong 50 epochs, LineVul 10 epochs, ReVeal max 100, IVDetect max 50 epochs, early stopping after 5 epochs without F1 gain (p. 6). For RQ1, DeepWukong is retrained on Big-Vul (28,294 vulnerable / 639,047 uncertain XFGs) to be comparable (p. 7). Balanced training = random undersampling of uncertain samples to equal vulnerable count (p. 8). Augmentation: eleven dead-code insertion strategies (details in online appendix) (p. 10). LLM fine-tuning hyper-parameters: not reported beyond "parameter-efficient fine-tuning" (p. 12). Seeds/repeats: not reported; authors state repeated training was not feasible (p. 13).
- Code availability: [A] scripts released (p. 2).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUC, each defined in the paper (p. 5). Per-SFP-cluster (CWE group) and per-severity F1 (p. 10–11).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] Mann-Whitney U tests for cyclomatic complexity (TP vs FP p = 0.043; TN vs FN p = 0.014) and for LIME positive-token ratio in FP vs TP (p = 0.13, α = 0.05) (p. 10). No CIs or tests for the main performance comparisons.

## 7. Key findings
1. Replication on original datasets: DeepWukong (SARD) P 87 / R 98 / F1 93 / AUC 88; LineVul (Big-Vul) P 96 / R 84 / F1 90 / AUC 85; ReVeal P 29 / R 59 / F1 38; IVDetect P 39 / R 63 / F1 24 (%) — [V] (p. 6, Table 2).
2. RQ1, original-trained models on Real-Vul test: DeepWukong P 1 / R 87 / F1 2 / AUC 62; LineVul P 1 / R 90 / F1 2 / AUC 58; ReVeal P 10 / R 80 / F1 17 / AUC 61; IVDetect P 2 / R 84 / F1 2 / AUC 59 (%) — [V] (p. 7, Table 3).
3. Drops vs original setting: precision −86 (DeepWukong), −95 (LineVul), −19 (ReVeal), −37 (IVDetect) pp; F1 −91, −88, −21, −22 pp — [V] (p. 7).
4. False positives on Real-Vul test: DeepWukong 439,494; LineVul 114,629; ReVeal 320,128; IVDetect 512,284 — [V] (p. 7).
5. RQ2, trained on imbalanced Real-Vul: DeepWukong and LineVul P/R/F1 0%, AUC 50% (predict everything uncertain); ReVeal F1 3%; IVDetect F1 0% — [V] (p. 8, Table 4).
6. RQ2, trained on balanced Real-Vul: F1 DeepWukong 2%, LineVul 20% (P 11, R 99), ReVeal 36% (P 31, R 45), IVDetect 6%; AUC 51.3–52.3% — [V] (p. 9, Table 5).
7. Dead-code augmentation: LineVul F1 20 → 46%, AUC 51.4 → 81.8%, precision 11 → 37%, recall 99 → 65%; smaller gains for graph models (DeepWukong F1 7%, ReVeal 38%, IVDetect 16%) — [V] (p. 10, Table 6).
8. Fine-tuned LLMs (with augmented training data): CodeLlama P 34 / R 54 / F1 42 / AUC 67; Mixtral P 38 / R 59 / F1 46 / AUC 71 (%). AUC lags LineVul by 14.8 and 10.8 pp; authors conclude "specialized tools (LineVul) outperform general large language models (LLMs)" — [V] numbers, [A] conclusion (p. 12, Table 8).
9. Per-CWE cluster: best F1 for information-leak (SFP 895, up to 33.6%) and tainted-input (896, 23.31%) clusters; worst for path resolution (893), predictability (905) and miscellaneous (907, no detections) — [V] (p. 10–11, Fig. 5). Cluster frequency strongly uneven (890 32%, 896 25%, 892 14%; 907 0.003%) — [V] (p. 11).
10. Per severity F1: high-severity vulnerabilities hardest (9.06–10.89%) vs medium (17.46–26.57%) and low (15.08–21.66%); only 5% of vulnerabilities are high severity — [V] (p. 10–11, Table 7).
11. Larger projects show lower false-positive rates (Fig. 4); higher cyclomatic complexity associated with FPs (p = 0.043) — [V] (p. 9–10).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Some Big-Vul vulnerable samples may be mislabelled, though Big-Vul labels were manually verified by Fan et al. (p. 13).
- [A] Only ten open-source projects; may not represent all real-world scenarios (p. 13).
- [A] "Uncertain" functions may contain undiscovered vulnerabilities (p. 13).
- [A] Balanced datasets use one random undersample; multiple runs were not feasible due to compute (p. 13).
- [A] Hash-based label-consistency check may miss whitespace variants despite regex normalisation (p. 13).
- [A] Only DL techniques evaluated; static and dynamic analysis tools left for future work (p. 13).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Internal numerical inconsistencies: (a) IVDetect replication reports P 39 / R 63 but F1 24 (the harmonic mean of 39 and 63 is ~48) (p. 6, Table 2); (b) Table 1 project sizes total 270,919 functions while the text reports 1,682,713 uncertain functions (p. 4, p. 13); (c) balanced LineVul shows R 99% with AUC 51.4% (p. 9, Table 5), which is hard to reconcile with high recall at ~99% accuracy. These do not change the qualitative story but make exact numbers less reliable.
- [I] The LLM comparison is thin and partly contradicts its own conclusion: Mixtral's F1 (46%) equals augmented LineVul's F1 (46%) and its precision (38%) is higher than LineVul's (37%); only AUC favours LineVul (p. 10, p. 12). The LLM accuracy of 80–83% at 34–38% precision implies a test set far less imbalanced than the 1,110 / 913,249 Real-Vul test set, so the LLM test set appears to differ from the DL test set (inferred from Table 8 vs p. 4); test-set composition and hyper-parameters are not reported. Mixtral is described as "7 B parameter", which [I] understates its 8×7B mixture-of-experts size.
- [I] RQ1 conflates two shifts: from commit-sampled to whole-project negatives (realistic base rate) and from original training data to a different test distribution; RQ2 isolates the first, and still yields F1 ≤ 36%.
- [I] Big-Vul is the label source for Real-Vul vulnerable functions; Ding et al. estimate only ~25% of Big-Vul vulnerable labels are correct [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4], so the authors' reliance on Fan et al.'s verification (p. 13) is optimistic.
- [I] Absolute false-positive counts are reported in different units (XFGs, chunks, CPGs, PDGs) per model (p. 7), so they are not directly comparable across models.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Temporal split and MD5-based label consistency reduce leakage; near-duplicates and inherited Big-Vul label noise remain. Single random undersample for balancing.
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] Ten large C/C++ projects dominated by Chromium and Linux; only function-level DL models plus two 7B-class LLMs; no SAST tools; no other languages.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Precision at realistic base rate is the practically relevant metric and is the paper's key contribution; AUC values near 50% with high recall suggest threshold effects. "Uncertain" negatives may hide real vulnerabilities, depressing measured precision.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No CIs or repeated runs for performance; Mann-Whitney tests only in side analyses, no multiple-comparison correction.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [A] Dataset and scripts on Zenodo (p. 2); [I] augmentation strategies and LLM fine-tuning settings only in an online appendix / not reported.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A] (p. 10–13): augmentations inducing structural/data-flow changes for graph models; better data strategies and architectures for contextual and system-level vulnerabilities; improving detection of high-severity vulnerabilities; improving LLM specificity for vulnerability detection; evaluating static and dynamic analysis tools on Real-Vul.
- Suggested by us [I]: run SAST tools and prompted/fine-tuned LLMs on the identical Real-Vul test set and report precision at a fixed alert budget; combine Real-Vul's whole-project negatives with PrimeVul-style label verification.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]: Strongest evidence in our set that base-rate realism (whole-project scanning) destroys precision of DL detectors (to 1–10%), complementing Ding et al.'s label/duplication findings. Gives per-CWE-cluster and severity breakdowns for RQ4, and a small fine-tuned-LLM vs LineVul comparison for RQ1 whose conclusion depends on the metric (AUC favours LineVul, F1 tied). Explicitly names SAST comparison on Real-Vul as missing (RQ5).

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ2 | Evaluated on whole-project, time-split Real-Vul, DL detectors' precision drops by up to 95 pp (to 1–10%) and F1 by up to 91 pp vs their original benchmarks | 7 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | 15% of vulnerable samples in the ReVeal dataset also appear as uncertain (label inconsistency) | 3 | A | weak |
| RQ1 | Even trained on balanced Real-Vul, DL detectors reach only F1 2–36% and AUC 51–52% on realistic test data | 9 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | Fine-tuned CodeLlama/Mixtral F1 42%/46%, AUC 67%/71% vs augmented LineVul F1 46%, AUC 81.8% (LLM test-set composition unclear) | 12 | V | weak |
| RQ4 | DL detectors detect information-leak and tainted-input CWE clusters best (F1 up to 33.6%) and path-traversal/predictability/misc clusters worst (none detected for SFP 907) | 11 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | High-severity vulnerabilities get the lowest F1 (9.06–10.89%) across all four models | 11 | V | moderate |
| RQ3 | Dead-code augmentation raises LineVul F1 20 → 46% and AUC 51.4 → 81.8% on Real-Vul | 10 | V | weak |
| RQ5 | Authors call for evaluating static and dynamic analysis tools on Real-Vul (not done) | 13 | A | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "precision declining by up to 95 percentage points and F1 scores dropping by up to 91 percentage points" (p. 1)

> "The study shows that specialized tools (LineVul) outperform general large language models (LLMs) in vulnerability detection" (p. 12)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: whole paper read (abstract to conclusion, references skimmed, author bios skipped). Scatter plots (Fig. 2–3) and the per-cluster bar charts (Fig. 5) were interpreted from the text only; cluster F1 maxima taken from the text on p. 10–11.
- Source version: arXiv 2407.03093v1 (3 Jul 2024), an "Author pre-print copy" of the TSE 2024 paper (p. 1). Page refs are to the arXiv PDF.
- Uncertainties: the numerical inconsistencies listed in section 9; how the LLM test set in Table 8 was built; "Real-Vul" uncertain-function count (1.68M vs 270,919).

# Top Score on the Wrong Exam: On Benchmarking in Machine Learning for Vulnerability Detection

- Authors: Risse, Niklas; Liu, Jing; Böhme, Marcel
- Year / venue: 2025, Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (published)
- DOI: 10.1145/3728887 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3728887
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] To examine whether the dominant problem statement of machine learning for vulnerability detection (ML4VD) — "given a function, does it contain a security flaw?" — is well-defined, by measuring how often function vulnerability can be decided without external context in popular datasets, and to explain why ML4VD models nevertheless score highly (p. 1–2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] Survey questions: what proportion of ML4VD papers use a function-level problem statement; which datasets they use (p. 3).
- [A] RQ.1 Can vulnerability detection be cast as function-level binary classification? (a) noisy labels, (b) context-dependent vulnerability, (c) context-dependent security of secure-labelled functions. RQ.2 Can high classification performance be achieved when the vulnerability's root cause is hidden (spurious features)? (p. 5).
- [A] Hypothesis: vulnerability of a function often cannot be decided without context (p. 1).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] (1) Literature survey of 2020–2024 ML4VD papers at ICSE, FSE, ASE, ISSTA, S&P, USENIX Security, NDSS, CCS, TSE, TOSEM, TIFS, TDSC, following Kitchenham/Petersen guidelines; >2,500 candidates → 109 by title → 81 by abstract/full text, filtered by one co-author (p. 3–4). (2) Manual labelling study by two security researchers with a 15-minute decision cap per function, plus a second round on context dependence (p. 6–7). (3) Constructing artificial vulnerable contexts for secure-labelled functions (p. 10). (4) Training a Gradient Boosting Classifier on word counts only (p. 7, p. 11).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Gradient Boosting Classifier on word-count features with no code structure, no pre-training; trained on each dataset's training subset and evaluated on its evaluation subset (p. 7, p. 11).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Published state-of-the-art scores: SNOPY 67.86% F1 and PDBERT 67.61% accuracy on Devign; DeepDFA 96.46% F1 on BigVul; CodeT5 Small 48.28% F1 on DiverseVul (Chen et al. benchmark) (p. 7). [V] SOTA values are taken from the literature, not re-run. [V] No LLM or static-analysis tool is evaluated experimentally (p. 7).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] BigVul, Devign (most used in survey) and DiverseVul (recent, widely used in preprints); ReVeal excluded because it lacks patch-commit IDs/CVEs (p. 6).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 100 randomly sampled vulnerable-labelled functions per dataset (300 total) from patch commits 2010–2022 covering 80 projects (BigVul 25, Devign 2, DiverseVul 60) (p. 6). 30 secure-labelled functions per dataset (90 total) for RQ.1-c (p. 10). Survey: 81 papers (p. 4). Class balance: Devign 47.9%, BigVul 4.5%, DiverseVul 5.4% vulnerable (p. 7).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Random sampling; sample size "inspired by" Croft et al. (n=70) (p. 6). No power analysis.
- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Scripts, sampled functions, labels and explanations at https://github.com/niklasrisse/TopScoreWrongExam (p. 6–7, p. 13).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Annotators reviewed patch commit and, where available, CVE report; >150 hours total; labels Secure / Vulnerable / No decision; ambiguous callee-vs-caller fixes labelled callee only (p. 6). [V] Inter-rater agreement: 82% (Cohen's κ = 0.64) for vulnerable/secure; 98% (κ = 0.96) for context dependence; disagreements resolved by discussion (p. 6). [V] Annotators: 3 and 5 years security research experience; second annotator co-discovered three CVEs present in the datasets (p. 6–7). [V] Classifier training+evaluation took 30 minutes on a MacBook Pro (p. 11). GBC hyper-parameters and the exact train/evaluation splits: not reported in the paper text.
- Code availability: [A] GitHub repository above (p. 7).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] F1 as primary metric because it dominates the surveyed literature; accuracy only for balanced Devign, omitted for imbalanced BigVul/DiverseVul (p. 7). [V] Labelling outcomes reported as proportions; Cohen's kappa for agreement (p. 6).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported beyond Cohen's kappa; no CIs on proportions.

## 7. Key findings
1. 88% of 81 surveyed ML4VD papers (2020–2024) define ML4VD as function-level binary classification (SE conferences 92%, security conferences 75%, journals 85%); 95% in 2024 — [V] (p. 5, Fig. 2a).
2. BigVul and Devign are each used by 36 papers and ReVeal by 22; 53 of 81 papers use at least one of the three — [V] (p. 5, Fig. 3).
3. Label accuracy of vulnerable-labelled functions: BigVul 39%, Devign 47%, DiverseVul 65% actually vulnerable (Devign 3% no decision) — [V] (p. 7–8, Fig. 6).
4. Reasons for wrong labels: patch-commit identification (BigVul 21%, Devign 54%, DiverseVul 3%), structural changes caused by the fix (48%, 38%, 66%), unrelated changes (31%, 8%, 31%) — [V] (p. 8, Table I).
5. All 151 truly vulnerable functions were context-dependent; none could be decided from the function alone — [V] (p. 9).
6. Types of context dependence: external functions 43–52%, function arguments 40–47%, globals 2–10%, type declarations 0–3%, execution environment 0–3% — [V] (p. 9, Table II).
7. For 82 of 90 secure-labelled functions the authors could construct a context in which the function is vulnerable — [V] (p. 10).
8. Word-count Gradient Boosting vs SOTA: BigVul F1 0.86 vs 0.96; Devign F1 0.62 vs 0.68 and accuracy 0.63 vs 0.68; DiverseVul F1 0.11 vs 0.48 — [V] (p. 11, Table III).
9. Authors conclude the function-level problem statement is ill-defined, "there is currently no evidence that ML4VD techniques are actually capable of identifying security vulnerabilities at the function-level", and high scores likely reflect spurious correlations — [A] (p. 2, p. 11–12).
10. Authors argue intra-procedural static analysis faces the same context-dependency problem and that combining static analysis with ML is promising — [A] (p. 2, p. 12–13).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Selection bias from random sampling of 100 functions per dataset (p. 11).
- [A] Manual labelling is subjective; some human error may remain despite cross-labelling (p. 11–12).
- [A] Only three datasets; may not generalise to other datasets or real-world systems (p. 12).
- [A] Datasets are mainly C; may not generalise to other languages (p. 12).
- [A] Only the function-level problem statement studied; other granularities need similar study (p. 12).
- [A] Spurious correlation shown only with word counts; other spurious features need study (p. 12). The GBC result shows datasets can be exploited, not that SOTA models actually do so (p. 11).
- [A] Secure functions were not verified to be truly non-vulnerable (p. 10).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] The context-dependence criterion is very permissive: almost any function that dereferences a pointer or uses an argument can be made vulnerable by an adversarial caller (e.g. passing NULL, Fig. 11, p. 10). The 100% / 82-of-90 results are partly a consequence of this definition and say more about the problem framing than about any detector.
- [I] Word-count GBC vs SOTA compares a model the authors trained with literature numbers produced under possibly different splits and preprocessing (p. 7, p. 11); no re-run of SOTA models on identical splits, no repeated runs, and GBC settings are not given.
- [I] On DiverseVul (the least leaky/noisy of the three per Ding et al.) word counts reach only 0.11 F1 vs 0.48 (p. 11); the spurious-feature argument is therefore strongest for BigVul/Devign, not universal.
- [I] Label-accuracy samples are small (n=100; ~±10 pp at 95% binomial CI by our calculation) and κ = 0.64 for the first step is only "substantial"; the 15-minute cap may bias towards "secure" for complex cases.
- [I] Survey screening was done by a single author (p. 4), a risk for selection consistency.
- [I] No LLM or SAST experiment: relevance to LLM-vs-SAST is through benchmark validity, not head-to-head numbers.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Random sampling and released labels are strengths; single-screener survey and annotators' prior work on ML4VD critique (refs [19], [24]) could bias judgements towards the hypothesis.
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] Three C/C++ datasets; Devign sample spans only 2 projects (p. 6); results may differ for Java/Python or curated datasets such as PrimeVul.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] "Context-dependent" is not a measure of detector failure; a context-dependent vulnerability may still be statistically predictable from code patterns. The word-count probe tests exploitability of datasets, not model behaviour.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No CIs; per-dataset proportions from n=100 (vulnerable) and n=30 (secure).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [A] Full artifact (scripts, samples, labels, explanations) released (p. 13).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A] (p. 12–13): binary classification with abstention; other base units (lines, files, modules, inter-procedural slices); context-conditional classification with the full repository at the patch commit as context; replacing classification by generating a vulnerable context or an ML-assisted proof-of-vulnerability test case; combining static analysis and ML; methods to detect spurious correlations in benchmarks.
- Suggested by us [I]: test whether LLMs given repository-level context (or tool-augmented with static analysis) reduce the context-dependency problem on the released labelled subset; repeat the word-count probe on PrimeVul and Real-Vul.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2, RQ3, RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]: Key methodological critique for RQ2 — explains why high F1 on BigVul/Devign (used by most DL and many LLM papers) is weak evidence of detection ability: labels are 39–65% accurate, vulnerability is context-dependent, and word counts reach near-SOTA scores. Supports interpreting fu2023chatgpt's 94% F1 for fine-tuned models as benchmark-inflated. For RQ3/RQ5 it argues for context-aware formulations and static-analysis + ML combinations, but provides no experimental evidence on hybrids.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ2 | 88% of 81 ML4VD papers (2020–2024, top venues) frame detection as function-level binary classification; 53/81 use BigVul, Devign or ReVeal | 5 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Only 39% (BigVul), 47% (Devign) and 65% (DiverseVul) of sampled vulnerable-labelled functions are actually vulnerable (n=100 each) | 8 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | All 151 truly vulnerable functions required context beyond the function (mainly external functions 43–52% and arguments 40–47%) | 9 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | A word-count Gradient Boosting classifier reaches F1 0.86 on BigVul (SOTA 0.96) and 0.62 on Devign (SOTA 0.68), but only 0.11 on DiverseVul (SOTA 0.48) | 11 | V | moderate |
| RQ5 | Authors argue there is currently no evidence that ML4VD techniques can identify vulnerabilities at function level | 2 | A | moderate |
| RQ3 | Authors argue function-level static analysis faces the same context problem and propose combining static analysis with ML | 12 | A | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "there is currently no evidence that ML4VD techniques are actually capable of identifying security vulnerabilities at the function-level" (p. 2)

> "All 151 vulnerable functions in our empirical study required additional context to be identified." (p. 9)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: whole paper read (survey, study design, results, threats, discussion, data availability); reference list skimmed. Survey figures (Fig. 2–4) read via text values.
- Source version: arXiv 2408.12986v2 (23 Apr 2025); published in Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (FSE 2025), DOI above. Page refs are to the arXiv PDF.
- Uncertainties: GBC hyper-parameters and the exact train/evaluation splits used for the word-count probe are not stated in the paper text (may be in the artifact). The abstract's ">90% of functions" combines vulnerable (151/151) and secure (82/90) results.

# ChatGPT for Vulnerability Detection, Classification, and Repair: How Far Are We?

- Authors: Fu, Michael; Tantithamthavorn, Chakkrit Kla; Nguyen, Van; Le, Trung
- Year / venue: 2023, 2023 30th Asia-Pacific Software Engineering Conference (APSEC) (published)
- DOI: 10.1109/apsec60848.2023.00085 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/apsec60848.2023.00085
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] To assess how well prompted ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo and gpt-4) performs on four vulnerability tasks (function- and line-level vulnerability prediction, CWE-type classification, CVSS severity estimation, vulnerability repair) compared with smaller language models fine-tuned for these tasks (p. 1).
- [A] Motivation: ChatGPT's weights are proprietary, so the authors cannot fine-tune it; the comparison is therefore prompted ChatGPT vs fine-tuned code LMs (p. 1).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] RQ1 accuracy of ChatGPT for function- and line-level vulnerability prediction; RQ2 for vulnerability-type (CWE-ID) classification; RQ3 for severity (CVSS) estimation; RQ4 for automated vulnerability repair (p. 1–2).
- No formal hypotheses.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Benchmark comparison on held-out test splits of existing datasets; ChatGPT used via prompting through the paid OpenAI API; baselines replicated with the original authors' parameter settings (p. 3).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] gpt-3.5-turbo and gpt-4 with task prompts (Fig. 1–4). Detection: task description plus return-format instruction; for vulnerable functions a follow-up prompt asks for the top-10 most vulnerability-prone lines (p. 2). Classification: ChatGPT is told the function is vulnerable and given a list of candidate CWE-IDs (p. 2). Repair: prompt includes three repair examples (p. 3). [I] The detection prompt appears to be zero-shot (based on the description on p. 2; the prompt itself is only shown as a figure).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] AIBugHunter (fine-tuned LMs, ~120M parameters), CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT (all fine-tuned); VulExplainer added for CWE classification (p. 3–4). [V] No static-analysis (SAST) tool baseline is included (p. 3).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Big-Vul (Fan et al.) for RQ1–RQ3: 188k C/C++ functions from 348 GitHub projects, 3,754 vulnerabilities across 91 types, vulnerable functions labelled with CWE-ID and CVSS score, vulnerable:benign ratio 1:20 (p. 3). [V] Big-Vul + CVEFixes as pre-processed by Chen et al. for repair: 5.5k vulnerable-function/patch pairs (p. 3).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] Function. Big-Vul split 80/10/10 (train/val/test); repair data split 70/10/20 (p. 3). The number of test functions actually submitted to ChatGPT is not reported.
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Split "similar to previous studies" (p. 3); no de-duplication or time-based split is reported.
- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Dataset, prompts and results published at https://github.com/awsm-research/ChatGPT4Vul (p. 1).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Baselines replicated with original settings on AMD Ryzen 9 5950X, 64 GB RAM, RTX 3090 (p. 3). [V] Greedy decoding for fine-tuned repair models "to ensure a fair comparison with ChatGPT" (p. 5). ChatGPT temperature, model snapshot/date and number of runs: not reported.
- Code availability: [A] repository above (p. 1).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] F1, precision, recall (function level) and top-10 accuracy (share of vulnerable functions with at least one true vulnerable line in the top-10 ranking), following LineVul (p. 3); multiclass accuracy for CWE classification (p. 4); MSE and MAE for CVSS v3.1 estimation (p. 4); %PP (exact match with ground-truth patch), BLEU and METEOR for repair (p. 4–5).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported (single point estimates in bar charts).

## 7. Key findings
1. Function-level detection, Big-Vul test split, F1: AIBugHunter 94%, CodeBERT 87%, GraphCodeBERT 35%, gpt-4 29%, gpt-3.5-turbo 10% — [V] (p. 4, Fig. 5; text p. 3).
2. Precision: AIBugHunter 98%, CodeBERT 92%, GraphCodeBERT 50%, gpt-4 25%, gpt-3.5-turbo 11%. Recall: AIBugHunter 90%, CodeBERT 83%, gpt-4 33%, GraphCodeBERT 27%, gpt-3.5-turbo 9% — [V] (p. 4, Fig. 5).
3. Line-level top-10 accuracy: AIBugHunter 99%, CodeBERT 99%, GraphCodeBERT 87%, gpt-4 65%, gpt-3.5-turbo 25% — [V] (p. 4, Fig. 5; text p. 3).
4. CWE-ID classification accuracy: fine-tuned baselines 62–65% (AIBugHunter 65%, VulExplainer 65%, CodeBERT 63%, GraphCodeBERT 62%) vs gpt-4 20% and gpt-3.5-turbo 13% — [V] (p. 4, Fig. 6).
5. CVSS severity: MSE 1.8–1.86 for fine-tuned baselines vs 5.4 (gpt-3.5-turbo) and 5.85 (gpt-4); MAE 0.83–0.93 vs 1.84 and 1.86 — [V] (p. 4, Fig. 7).
6. Repair %PP: AIBugHunter (VulRepair) 30, GraphCodeBERT 9, CodeBERT 7, gpt-3.5-turbo 0, gpt-4 0 — [V] (p. 5, Fig. 8).
7. Despite ~14,000× more parameters than CodeBERT, ChatGPT needs domain-specific fine-tuning to generalise to vulnerability tasks — [A] (p. 1, p. 5).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] None. The paper has no limitations or threats-to-validity section; the only constraint mentioned is that ChatGPT's parameters are proprietary and cannot be fine-tuned (p. 1).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Short paper (5 PDF pages including references): method detail is thin — number of test samples sent to ChatGPT, temperature, model snapshot dates, repeated runs and the full detection prompt text are not given in the text.
- [I] Evaluation uses a random Big-Vul split with no de-duplication or temporal split. Ding et al. report 12.7% exact-copy leakage and ~25% label accuracy for Big-Vul vulnerable functions, and Risse et al. reach 86% F1 on Big-Vul from word counts alone; both suggest the 94% F1 of the fine-tuned baseline is inflated by dataset artefacts that in-distribution fine-tuning can exploit but prompting cannot. The size of the LLM-vs-fine-tuned gap may therefore partly reflect benchmark artefacts (based on [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4] and [@risse2025top, p. 11]).
- [I] Asymmetric comparison: baselines are fine-tuned on Big-Vul training data, ChatGPT is prompted. The result answers "prompting vs in-distribution fine-tuning", not "LLM vs DL" in general.
- [I] The first two authors also built the strongest baselines (AIBugHunter, LineVul, VulRepair, VulExplainer — refs [8]–[11], p. 5). Not a funding conflict, but the comparison favours the authors' own tools and should be read with that in mind.
- [I] GraphCodeBERT F1 35% vs CodeBERT 87% on the same data is an unusually large gap that the paper does not discuss (p. 4, Fig. 5); the dagger marks on CodeBERT/GraphCodeBERT in Fig. 5–7 are not explained in the text.
- [I] %PP (exact match) is a very strict repair metric; 0% for ChatGPT may partly reflect format mismatch with Chen et al.'s patch representation, which the authors tried to mitigate with three in-prompt examples (p. 3).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Random Big-Vul split without reported de-duplication → possible train/test leakage that only benefits the fine-tuned baselines; prompt design not tuned or ablated; single run.
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] C/C++ only, one detection dataset, one 2023 snapshot of each ChatGPT model; results may not transfer to newer LLMs, other prompting strategies or other languages.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] F1 on a 1:20 dataset whose vulnerable labels are largely inaccurate per later audits, so "correct" predictions need not be detected vulnerabilities; %PP measures textual identity, not functional correctness.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No variance, confidence intervals or significance tests; LLM outputs are non-deterministic and only one run is implied.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [A] Data, prompts and results released (p. 1); [I] model versions and temperature are not stated, and hosted OpenAI models change over time.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A] (p. 5): fine-tuning on domain-specific data is "crucial" for ChatGPT to generalise to vulnerability repair, and "pivotal" for vulnerability tasks in general.
- Suggested by us [I]: re-run the prompted-LLM vs fine-tuned comparison on a de-duplicated, temporally split, label-verified benchmark (e.g. PrimeVul), add a SAST baseline, and report variance across repeated LLM runs.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4.
- How it informs our work [I]: An early, widely cited head-to-head of prompted ChatGPT vs fine-tuned code LMs showing a large gap in favour of fine-tuned models on Big-Vul. For RQ2 it illustrates how a random-split Big-Vul evaluation can make fine-tuned models look near-perfect. It should be read together with ding2025vulnerability, where on PrimeVul paired functions the ordering reverses (GPT models beat fine-tuned models on pair-wise correctness, although all are at or below random guessing).

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | On Big-Vul (random split), prompted gpt-4 F1 29% and gpt-3.5-turbo F1 10% vs fine-tuned AIBugHunter 94% and CodeBERT 87% for function-level detection | 4 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | Line-level top-10 accuracy: gpt-4 65%, gpt-3.5-turbo 25% vs AIBugHunter/CodeBERT 99% | 4 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | CWE-ID classification accuracy: ChatGPT 13–20% vs fine-tuned models 62–65% (C/C++, Big-Vul) | 4 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | ChatGPT produced 0% exact-match repairs vs 7–30% for fine-tuned models | 5 | V | weak |
| RQ2 | Evaluation used an 80/10/10 Big-Vul split (1:20 ratio) with no de-duplication or temporal split reported | 3 | V | moderate |
| RQ5 | Authors argue prompted LLMs lack security domain knowledge and need fine-tuning for vulnerability tasks | 5 | A | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "the fine-tuned AIBugHunter achieves an F1-measure of 94% along with a top-10 accuracy of 99% with only 120 million parameters" (p. 3)

> "ChatGPT failed to generate correct repair patches for all of the vulnerable functions in our testing data." (p. 5)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: whole paper read (5 PDF pages: abstract, introduction, related work, prompt design, experiments, conclusion, references). Bar-chart values in Fig. 5–8 were read from the rendered PDF pages 4–5 because text extraction garbles the axis labels.
- Source version: arXiv 2310.09810v1 (15 Oct 2023); the published version is APSEC 2023 (DOI above). Page refs are to the arXiv PDF; small differences from the APSEC version are possible.
- Short paper (5 pages, self-described "pilot study", p. 2): weight accordingly in synthesis.
- Uncertainties: ChatGPT test-set size, full detection prompt (figure only), model snapshot dates and temperature are not reported. In Fig. 5 gpt-4 recall (33%) is above GraphCodeBERT (27%) although its F1 is lower — values read from the rendered figure.

# A Systematic Literature Review on Detecting Software Vulnerabilities with Large Language Models

- Authors: Kaniewski, Sabrina; Schmidt, Fabian; Enzweiler, Markus; Menth, Michael; Heer, Tobias
- Year / venue: 2026, ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (published)
- DOI: 10.1145/3815425 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3815425
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
- **Version analysed:** arXiv:2507.22659v2 (19 Dec 2025) (p. 1), the preprint of the TOSEM article (DOI 10.1145/3815425), not the typeset journal version. Study statistics are "as of December 13th 2025" (p. 8).

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

Convention for this survey: two kinds of numbers are marked [V]: counts about the review's own corpus shown in its own tables and figures, and dataset statistics that the authors recomputed from the published datasets (Table 5 states the numbers "are reproduced with the officially published datasets", p. 28). They are the review's own data, although we cannot re-check the extraction. Anything reported about results of individual primary studies is second-hand and marked [A], never [V].

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Map the fragmented field of LLM-based software vulnerability detection. The authors argue that studies are hard to compare because of different system designs, datasets, metrics and splits (p. 1–2).
- [A] Contributions (p. 2–3):
  - an SLR of 263 studies (Jan 2020–Nov 2025)
  - a taxonomy covering task formulation, input representation, system architecture, adaptation/orchestration technique and dataset usage
  - an in-depth dataset analysis (class balance, CWE coverage/diversity)
  - limitations and future directions
  - a living public repository (Awesome-LLM4SVD)
- [A] The term "LLM" is used broadly and includes small pre-trained models such as BERT and CodeBERT (footnote, p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- RQ1: How is the detection task formulated in LLM-based systems? (p. 6)
- RQ2: How are input and vulnerability semantics represented for LLMs? (p. 6)
- RQ3: What are the predominant techniques for adapting LLMs to detection? (p. 6)
- RQ4: Which datasets are used, and how does dataset selection affect applicability? (p. 6)
- RQ5: How does dataset selection affect comparability across studies? (p. 6)
- No hypotheses.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: SLR following Kitchenham et al. guidelines (p. 5). It has three phases: literature search, study selection and study analysis (Fig. 1, p. 8).
- Search: automated search of IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library and arXiv on titles/abstracts (p. 6–7). The full Boolean search string is printed: LLM/model-family terms AND (vulnerability/CVE/CWE) AND (detect*/identif*/classif*/analy*/discover*/assess*) AND (software/program/code) (p. 7). The initial search ran in December 2024, followed by continuous database alerts and scholar.inbox notifications (p. 7).
- Inclusion criteria [A]: title or abstract matches the search string; the study uses **and evaluates** LLMs for software vulnerability detection and introduces novel techniques or systems (Table 2, p. 8).
- Exclusion criteria [A] (Table 2, p. 8; p. 7):
  - not in English, or full text not accessible
  - reviews, surveys, theses, abstracts, posters, demos, tutorials
  - binary code, smart contracts, network analysis or malware
  - studies that use LLMs **only to work on outputs of other tools (e.g. SAST)**
  - LLMs mentioned only in passing or used merely as baselines
  - duplicates or extended versions
- Quality assessment [A]: a manual check of contribution, workflow/implementation description, evaluation setup (datasets, baselines, metrics) and coherence of findings, motivated by the inclusion of preprints (p. 7). The scoring scheme, threshold and number of excluded studies are not reported.
- Snowballing: backward (reference lists) and forward (Google Scholar citations), with snowballed studies passing the same criteria (p. 7).
- Extraction: task definition, LLMs used, adaptation techniques, input representation, datasets, targeted CWEs and metrics (p. 7–8).
- Number of reviewers, independent double screening and inter-rater agreement: not reported.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: not applicable. The review does **not** synthesise LLM-vs-SAST or LLM-vs-DL performance. Studies that use LLMs only as baselines are excluded (p. 8).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): ACM DL (514 hits), IEEE Xplore (865), arXiv (2,776) [V] (Fig. 1, p. 8). Screening counts per stage (title/abstract, full text, quality, snowballing) are not reported.
- Sample size (N) and unit: 263 primary studies [V] (p. 7–8): 185 peer-reviewed and 78 (29.7%) arXiv preprints [V] (p. 8; Fig. 2, p. 9). The earliest study is from 2020 (p. 8). The A*/A conference and Q1 journal venues are listed in Table 3, e.g. ICSE 13 and TSE 7 [V] (p. 9).
- Time window: January 2020 – November 2025 (p. 1–2).
- Dataset analysis: 20 datasets are characterised (the 15 most used plus 5 selected recent ones; Tables 4–5, p. 26, p. 28). 12 real-world/mixed multi-class datasets are analysed for CWE distribution, with D2A and FormAI excluded (p. 30).
- Data availability: artifacts and the categorised study list are in a public GitHub repository [144] (p. 3, p. 43).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, tools: full-text review with structured extraction (p. 7–8). The taxonomy categories are refined iteratively and aligned with existing definitions where possible (p. 43). CWE clustering uses the MITRE CWE-1000 Research View pillars (p. 30–32). Dataset usage is analysed over time (Fig. 11, p. 34), by co-usage pairs (Fig. 12, p. 35) and by overlap within use cases (Fig. 13, p. 36).
- Code availability: artifacts released [144] (p. 3).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - Study counts per taxonomy node, used to show prevalence.
  - Dataset size, % vulnerable samples and number of distinct CWEs, as proxies for label diversity and balance (p. 25, p. 28).
  - Share of CWE labels per CWE-1000 pillar and Top-25 CWE concentration, measuring thematic diversity (p. 31–32).
  - Dataset usage frequency and overlap, measuring comparability (p. 34–37).
- The review does not extract or pool the effectiveness metrics (precision/recall/F1) of primary studies, although "evaluation metrics" is listed among the extracted fields (p. 8).
- Statistical testing: none; not reported.

## 7. Key findings
1. Task formulation: binary classification dominates (195 studies). Vulnerability-specific classification: 20; multi-class: 61; multi-label: 23. Only a minority combine classification with generation tasks (description, root-cause reasoning, structured report) — [V] (p. 11; Fig. 4, p. 12)
2. Input: 139 studies feed raw code. Structured inputs (AST/CFG/DFG/PDG/CPG, slices, code gadgets) and auxiliary information (CWE lists, few-shot examples, execution context, SAST tool output) are used less often — [V] (p. 13–14)
3. Architecture and scale: decoder-only LLMs dominate. Tiny/small models (< 8B) are mostly full-parameter fine-tuned, while medium/large models are mostly prompted or PEFT-tuned. Hybrid LLM + GNN/RNN/CNN architectures form a distinct group — [V] (p. 15–16; Fig. 5, p. 16)
4. Advanced techniques are emerging but rare: RAG in 25 studies, LoRA in 27, agentic systems in 10, GNN hybrids in 20 — [V] (p. 36–37)
5. Dataset usage is concentrated on old function-level C/C++ benchmarks. Devign is used in 69 studies, Big-Vul in 63, ReVeal in 40, SARD in 32, DiverseVul and PrimeVul in 27 each — [V] (Table 4, p. 26)
6. Datasets are highly imbalanced. Recomputed vulnerable shares: Big-Vul 4.5%, DiverseVul 5.7%, PrimeVul 2.9%, D2A 1.4%, ReposVul 0.7%, compared with Devign 48.0% — [V] (Table 5, p. 28)
7. Real-world datasets follow a long-tail CWE distribution: the Top-25 CWEs account for about 80% of labels. Memory/resource-lifetime CWEs dominate, and several CWE-1000 pillars are absent from the Top 25 — [V] (p. 30, p. 32; Figs. 8–10)
8. 555 CWEs that are allowed for vulnerability mapping in CWE-1000 appear in none of the analysed datasets. Many dataset labels use discouraged or abstract CWEs (e.g. CWE-119, CWE-399, CWE-20) — [V] (p. 32, p. 34)
9. Fragmentation of evaluation setups:
   - 87 studies use or introduce custom datasets, and only nine datasets are reused in more than ten studies (p. 35).
   - Few datasets have predefined train/validation/test splits: Draper, CodeXGLUE-Devign, Big-Vul, PrimeVul (p. 39).
   - Among agentic studies, only 4 of 10 share PrimeVul (p. 37).

   — [V] for the counts, [A] for the conclusion that cross-study comparison is unreliable
10. Data leakage: widely used static benchmarks (Devign, Big-Vul) are likely in LLM pre-training corpora, so high scores may reflect memorisation rather than generalisation — [A] (p. 30, p. 38–39)
11. Robustness: models rely on superficial textual patterns, and performance degrades under semantics-preserving transformations (renaming, reordering, formatting) — [A] (p. 39)
12. Practical deployment: there are few evaluations in realistic development settings, models often underperform outside curated benchmarks (citing our `chakraborty2024revisiting`), and costs are high — [A] (p. 39–40)
13. LLM–SAST relationship. LLMs are presented as free of the hand-written, language-specific rules that SAST needs (p. 1, p. 12–13). In the corpus, SAST appears as auxiliary input to LLMs: tool output in prompts, or hybrid workflows where the LLM verifies or refines static-analysis findings ([18], [145], [219], [340], [365]) (p. 14, p. 18). The authors see synergy of LLMs with program analysis as "a current pathway for industrial adoption": SAST detects and the LLM filters false positives, or the LLM proposes and static analysis verifies (p. 42). This is qualitative only, with no quantified comparison — [A]

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Paper retrieval omissions (keywords, a static snapshot of a living field), mitigated by a broad search string, snowballing, continuous alerts and a maintained repository (p. 42–43).
- [A] Study selection bias, including the decision not to filter by venue rank and to include preprints. Mitigated by reporting venue tiers and a manual quality assessment (p. 43).
- [A] Subjectivity in data extraction and taxonomy classification (e.g. "reasoning" vs "description"). Mitigated by aligning with existing definitions and releasing the categorised study list (p. 43).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] It is a mapping study, not an effectiveness synthesis. No precision/recall/F1 or false-positive data are pooled or compared, so it cannot answer RQ1 directly. Its value for us is RQ2/RQ5. Based on sections 4–6 and the absence of any results tables.
- [I] Scope excludes much of the hybrid design space we care about. Studies that use LLMs only to post-process SAST output (e.g. false-positive filtering) are excluded (p. 7–8). The very hybrid that the authors recommend for industry (p. 42) is therefore out of the corpus. Our RQ3 needs primary studies such as `du2026reducing`, `xiong2026sifting` and `li2024iris`.
- [I] Only three databases are searched (IEEE, ACM, arXiv) (p. 6). Springer, Elsevier, Wiley and USENIX/NDSS are not searched directly, which partly explains the high arXiv hit count. Snowballing and alerts mitigate this only partly.
- [I] Opaque quality assessment and screening. The QA criteria are listed without a scoring scheme or threshold, and per-stage exclusion counts, number of reviewers and agreement are not reported (p. 7–8). This is weaker than `zhou2025large`'s explicit 0–3 scoring.
- [I] The broad LLM definition (BERT/CodeBERT counted as LLMs, p. 2) and the inclusion of feature-extraction-only uses (p. 17) blur the line between "LLM-based" and "pre-trained-transformer DL" detectors. That line matters for our three-way LLM vs SAST vs DL comparison.
- [I] Minor internal inconsistencies:
  - The Fig. 11 caption says "Jan 2020 to Mar 2025" while the text says Jan 2020 to Nov 2025 (p. 34).
  - SecurityEval is described with "75 CWE types" (p. 29) but 69 CWEs in Table 5 (p. 28) and on p. 30.
  - Ding et al. (PrimeVul) appears twice in the references, as [54] (arXiv) and [55] (ICSE) (p. 46).
  - The statement that large models "achieve state-of-the-art performance on vulnerability detection benchmarks" (p. 15) has no citation.

  None of these affects the main conclusions.
- [I] Preprint-heavy corpus: 29.7% of studies are arXiv preprints (p. 8). Corpus-level counts mix peer-reviewed and non-peer-reviewed work, and the counts are not split by peer-review status.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): selection is subjective and the screening reliability is not reported. The exclusion of "LLM on tool output" studies shapes conclusions about hybrids (p. 7). The review itself highlights data leakage as a key threat in primary studies (p. 24, p. 30, p. 38–39).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): source code only, with binaries, smart contracts and malware excluded (p. 8). The corpus is C/C++-heavy because the datasets are (p. 28, p. 37).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): the number of distinct CWEs is used as a proxy for label diversity (p. 25), and pillar mapping depends on the quality of NVD labels (p. 32). Counts of studies per technique measure popularity, not effectiveness.
- Statistical conclusion: not applicable (no inferential analysis).
- Reproducibility: strong for an SLR. The full search string is printed (p. 7), and the artifacts and categorised studies are public [144] (p. 3, p. 43). Screening records and QA scores are not reported.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A] (Table 7, p. 38; p. 40–42):
  - L1 Granularity: project- and repository-level detection; richer code context (callees, types, globals, execution/data flow); languages beyond C/C++ (Python, Java, Rust); multilingual and cross-project benchmarks (p. 40).
  - L2 Labels and quality: manual verification and better VFC labelling tools; reasoning-oriented benchmarks with verified root-cause explanations; datasets built after model knowledge cutoffs to avoid leakage; covering the 555 unused mappable CWEs (p. 40–41).
  - L3 Comparability: datasets with documented splits (or closed test sets); evaluating on multiple datasets (recent PrimeVul/MegaVul plus established Devign/Big-Vul); documenting all preprocessing; open science (p. 41).
  - L4 Up-to-date knowledge: automatically updated datasets (e.g. CVEfixes); RAG and continual learning (p. 41).
  - L5 Representation: structure-aware and language-agnostic inputs; LLM + GNN hybrids; robustness tests on perturbed or LLM-generated code (p. 41).
  - L6 Explainability: metrics for explanation trustworthiness; structured explanations (propagation paths); grounding via CWE hierarchies (p. 42).
  - L7 Integration (p. 42):
    - IDE/CI integration, field studies and evaluation on proprietary code
    - CWE-type classifiers
    - agentic self-assessment
    - SAST + LLM synergy in both directions (SAST then LLM false-positive filter; LLM then static-analysis verification)
    - model compression and on-premise small models
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - No direction asks for controlled, same-benchmark comparisons of LLMs against SAST tools and non-LLM DL detectors. This gap is consistent with `zhou2025large` and `sheng2025llms`, and is a candidate for our RQ5 gap section (requires a novelty check).
  - The recommended SAST + LLM pipelines (p. 42) are, by construction, outside this SLR's corpus. Evidence for them must come from studies this SLR excludes.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (strongest: dataset taxonomy, imbalance, CWE coverage, leakage, splits, fragmentation), RQ5 (L1–L7 limitations and directions), RQ4 (C/C++ bias, CWE long tail, missing pillars), RQ3 (qualitative: SAST output as LLM input; recommended hybrids). RQ1 is not answered.
- How it informs our work [I]: the most recent and largest SLR in our corpus (263 studies, to Nov 2025) and peer-reviewed (TOSEM). Its dataset analysis gives concrete, recomputed evidence for why reported numbers disagree across studies. That is the core of our RQ2: different benchmarks, extreme class-balance differences (0.7–50% vulnerable), long-tailed CWE coverage, missing splits, custom datasets and leakage. It supports the claim that head-to-head LLM-vs-SAST/DL evidence must be read benchmark by benchmark.

## 14. Key quotes
> "studies frequently adopt custom datasets, metrics, and data splits, making it difficult to assess progress, reproduce results, or compare models fairly" (p. 2)

> "Only nine datasets are reused in more than ten studies, highlighting the lack of a standardized suite of benchmark datasets" (p. 35)

> "Pipelines where SAST tools detect candidates and LLMs filter false positives can significantly reduce alert fatigue" (p. 42)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage:
  - All 43 body pages read: methodology, taxonomy (sections 4.1–4.4), datasets (section 5), limitations and road ahead (section 6), threats, conclusion.
  - Long citation lists inside the taxonomy sections were skimmed, not checked individually.
  - The reference list (p. 44–63) was consulted for refs [29], [42], [54]/[55], [145], [159], [172], [219], [304], [368] and [394].
  - Figures 4, 5 and 8–13 are partly garbled in the text layer, so counts were taken from the running text and from Tables 4–5.
- Version: arXiv v2 (19 Dec 2025). The published TOSEM version was not compared.
- Overlap with our corpus (cited as primary studies): `ahmed2026secvuleval` ([3]), `chakraborty2024revisiting` ([29]), `ding2025vulnerability` ([54]/[55]), `khare2025understanding` ([146]), `li2024iris` ([172]), `yildiz2025benchmarking` ([368]), `zhou2024comparison` ([394]). It also cites a separate LLM-vs-traditional-methods survey (Taghavi Far & Feyzi 2025, [304]) that is not in our project. That survey might be worth screening for RQ1.
- Funding / conflict of interest: DFG project 528745080 (p. 44). The first author's prior survey ([143]) seeded the search terms (p. 7).
- Uncertainties: per-stage screening numbers are unknown, and the quality-assessment threshold is unknown.

# Large Language Model for Vulnerability Detection and Repair: Literature Review and the Road Ahead

- Authors: Zhou, Xin; Cao, Sicong; Sun, Xiaobing; Lo, David
- Year / venue: 2025, ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (published)
- DOI: 10.1145/3708522 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3708522
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
- **Version analysed:** arXiv:2404.02525v3 (7 Oct 2024) (p. 1), not the typeset TOSEM version. Numbers and wording may differ slightly from the journal version.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

Convention for this survey: counts about the review's own corpus that appear in its own tables or figures are marked [V]. They are the review's own data, although we cannot re-check the underlying extraction. Anything the survey reports about the results of individual primary studies is second-hand and marked [A], never [V].

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Provide the first systematic literature review focused on how LLMs are used for source-code vulnerability detection **and** repair, identify limitations of existing studies and propose a research roadmap (p. 1, p. 2).
- [A] The authors position it against earlier reviews that covered ML/DL broadly (to 2016, 2020, May 2022) or covered LLMs for SE in general without detailing vulnerability tasks (p. 3).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- RQ1: What LLMs have been used for vulnerability detection and repair? (p. 5)
- RQ2: How are LLMs adapted for vulnerability detection? (p. 5)
- RQ3: How are LLMs adapted for vulnerability repair? (p. 5)
- RQ4: What are the characteristics of datasets and deployment strategies in these studies? (p. 5)
- No hypotheses; descriptive review.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: SLR "following the guide by Zhang et al." (p. 5). Two search arms: (a) manual search of 13 conferences (ICSE, ESEC/FSE, ASE, ISSTA, CCS, S&P, USENIX Security, NDSS, AAAI, IJCAI, ICML, NIPS, ICLR) and 4 journals (TOSEM, TSE, TDSC, TIFS), yielding 35 papers; (b) automated search of 7 databases yielding 1,500 records, with the search string derived from the manually found papers (p. 5; Fig. 2, p. 4). Then multi-phase screening, quality assessment and forward/backward snowballing (p. 6–7).
- Approach / model / intervention: descriptive classification (taxonomy) of LLMs (encoder-only, encoder-decoder, decoder-only, following Pan et al.) and of adaptation techniques: fine-tuning (data-centric, combination with program analysis, LLM + other DL modules, domain-specific pre-training, causal learning), prompt engineering (zero-/few-shot) and retrieval augmentation (p. 3–4, p. 9–14; Fig. 1, p. 2).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: not applicable (review). The review does **not** compare LLM approaches with SAST tools or non-LLM DL detectors. Studies using only GNN/RNN models were explicitly excluded (p. 6).
- Inclusion criteria [A]: English; full text accessible; peer-reviewed full paper in a conference or journal (arXiv preprints from 2023–2024 kept subject to a quality check); uses LLM techniques for source-code vulnerability detection or repair (p. 5).
- Exclusion criteria [A]: fewer than 5 pages; books, keynotes, technical reports, theses, tool demos, editorials; literature reviews and surveys; duplicates or similar studies by the same authors; no LLM use (e.g. GNN only); LLM mentioned only as future work; not source-code detection/repair (binary code, protocols and network excluded) (p. 5–6).
- Quality assessment [A]: five criteria, QAC1–QAC5 (prestigious venue; contribution; clear workflow/implementation; clear experiment details; findings support the claims). Each is scored 0–3, and studies need a total of at least 12 (80%) to be included. Unpublished preprints score 0 on the venue criterion but are kept if they still reach 12 (p. 6).
- Number of reviewers, independent screening, conflict resolution and inter-rater agreement: not reported.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): manual venue search plus IEEE Xplore (197), ACM DL (285), SpringerLink (266), Wiley (205), Web of Science (237), ScienceDirect (220), arXiv (90) [V] (Fig. 2, p. 4).
- Sample size (N) and unit: 58 primary studies [V] (p. 1, p. 7). Selection flow [V] (Fig. 2, p. 4; p. 6–7):
  - 1,535 records
  - 1,387 after the page filter
  - 1,332 after de-duplication
  - 212 after venue/title/abstract screening
  - 82 after full-text screening
  - 42 after quality assessment (37 published + 5 preprints)
  - 58 final, after adding 16 papers from snowballing (83 snowballing candidates)

  The abstract reports 43 published + 15 preprints (p. 1). Table 2 lists 40 detection studies (p. 10) and Table 3 lists 19 repair studies (p. 16) [V].
- Time window: January 2018 – March 2024 (p. 5). The earliest included study is from 2021, and 2024 accounts for 46.6% of studies [V] (p. 7).
- Sampling / selection method: see section 3. Snowballing is described as "lightweight" (p. 7).
- Data availability: search keywords are in an online appendix (Google Doc) (p. 5, ref [8]). Extraction sheet and per-study QA scores: not reported.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, tools: the data extraction and analysis section reports only the distribution of studies by year and venue (p. 7). The extraction form is not reported beyond the fields visible in Tables 2–3: LLM size, adaptation technique, input granularity, data labelling, user interaction and workflow integration (p. 10, p. 16).
- Code availability: not applicable; the online appendix covers keywords only (p. 5).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: frequency counts and percentages of LLM usage (92 LLM usages in detection, 45 in repair) and of adaptation techniques (p. 7–9, p. 14, p. 17). The review does not aggregate the precision, recall or F1 reported by primary studies.
- Statistical testing: none (descriptive review); not reported.

## 7. Key findings
1. Encoder-only LLMs dominate detection. CodeBERT accounts for 26.1% (24/92) of LLM usages and GPT-3.5 for 9.8% (9/92). By architecture: encoder-only 47.8% (44/92), decoder-only 23.9% (22/92), encoder-decoder 9.8% (9/92), commercial with undisclosed architecture 18.5% (17/92) — [V] (p. 7–8)
2. Detection adaptation: fine-tuning ≈73%, prompt engineering ≈17%, retrieval augmentation ≈10% of studies — [V] (p. 9, p. 14). Repair: fine-tuning ≈63%, prompting ≈37% — [V] (p. 14, p. 17)
3. Most detection studies work at function level. Only 7 address line level, none address class level, and one works at repo level ([130], which is our `zhou2024comparison`) — [V] (p. 17–18)
4. Detection datasets mostly use heuristic labels: functions changed by vulnerability-fixing commits are labelled vulnerable in their pre-fix version, and other functions are labelled clean. Prior work has shown these labels to be noisy — [A] (p. 18)
5. Repair datasets mostly lack test cases. The two studies that have them evaluate only 42 and 12 samples — [A] (p. 18)
6. None of the reviewed studies is integrated into developer workflows; all are evaluated offline on static historical data. Only one detection study ([113]) produces explanations for developers — [V] (Tables 2–3; p. 19)
7. The only LLM-vs-SAST evidence comes from [130]: SAST tools reach low detection rates with relatively few false positives, while LLMs detect more vulnerabilities but have high false-positive rates. This is second-hand, from a study by the same first and last authors — [A] (p. 22)
8. The best reported state of the art is cited as 67.6% accuracy for detection and 20% for repair (refs [56], [128]) — [A], second-hand (p. 20–21)
9. Cited studies report that LLMs are not robust to data perturbations ([116], [59]). Others report that LLMs struggle with rare CWE types and with inter-procedural or multi-unit vulnerabilities ([51], [84], [128], [129]) — [A] (p. 20–21)

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] The only threat to validity discussed is missing relevant studies because of incomplete keywords or varied LLM terminology. It is mitigated by manual venue selection, automated search and snowballing (p. 24).
- [A] Scope: future versions will add vulnerability localisation and assessment (p. 24).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Dated corpus. The search ends in March 2024 (p. 5), before most agentic, repository-level and LLM + SAST hybrid work. Findings such as "encoder-only dominates" may not hold for 2025–2026: `kaniewski2026systematic` and `sheng2025llms` already report decoder-only dominance. Based on the time window and comparison with the other two surveys in this project.
- [I] Very thin evidence on LLM vs SAST. The single repo-level comparison is the authors' own study ([130], Zhou … Lo, 2024; ref list p. 29). The roadmap's statement about SAST-vs-LLM trade-offs is therefore effectively self-citation, not a synthesis.
- [I] No comparison with non-LLM DL detectors. GNN/RNN-only studies are excluded (p. 6), so the review cannot answer whether LLMs beat DL detectors.
- [I] The quality assessment uses "published in a prestigious venue" (QAC1) as a criterion (p. 6). This mixes venue prestige with methodological quality and structurally penalises preprints.
- [I] Gaps in process transparency: the number of screeners, their agreement and the per-study QA scores are not reported, and the search string is only in an external Google Doc (p. 5).
- [I] Minor internal inconsistencies:
  - The RQ3 answer says "three commonly used techniques" but lists two (p. 17).
  - Limitation 2 opens with "For vulnerability repair" while discussing detection label noise (p. 19).
  - By our count, Tables 2 and 3 contain 57 unique study references (Fu et al. [27] and [29] appear in both), versus 58 stated.

  None of these changes the main conclusions.
- [I] Repair is half of the scope, so detection-specific depth (metrics, benchmarks, CWE coverage) is limited.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): selection could be biased by the venue-first strategy and the prestige-weighted QA. Whether one or several people screened each paper is not reported. The review itself flags contamination of LLM pre-training corpora as a concern for primary studies (p. 20).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): the corpus covers Jan 2018–Mar 2024 and source code only, no binaries (p. 5–6). It is dominated by function-level studies (Table 2, p. 10).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): the technique shares (≈73/17/10%) are given without a stated denominator (p. 9). The classification of studies into categories is not validated.
- Statistical conclusion: not applicable (no quantitative synthesis).
- Reproducibility: keywords are in an online appendix (p. 5). Extraction data and QA scores are not released (not reported).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]:
  - Curate a smaller, manually verified, living high-quality test set for vulnerability detection, e.g. by combining manually checked samples from several studies (p. 22).
  - Repository-level detection and repair using long-context LLMs, extending the initial repo-level SAST-vs-LLM comparison (p. 22).
  - Open-source LLMs customised for vulnerability data (p. 22).
  - LLM usages not yet explored: agents, external tool use, advanced RAG (iterative, recursive, adaptive) (p. 22–23).
  - Deployment-ready features: developer interaction, explanations, IDE/VCS integration (p. 23).
  - Benchmarks with no overlap with LLM pre-training corpora, to avoid data contamination (p. 20).
  - Handling complex vulnerabilities: inter-procedural, rare CWE types, vulnerabilities spanning multiple code units (p. 20).
  - Vision for 2030: line- to repo-level detection and repair, evaluated on an expert-annotated benchmark (p. 23).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Check whether the agent, tool-use and repo-level directions proposed here have since been realised. Our corpus contains `guo2025repoaudit`, `li2024iris`, `yildiz2025benchmarking` and `li2026llm`.
  - Check whether the SAST-vs-LLM trade-off reported by `zhou2024comparison` (higher detection for LLMs, but more false positives) replicates in independent studies.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (dataset labelling, granularity, contamination) and RQ5 (limitations and roadmap). Marginally RQ1 (one second-hand SAST-vs-LLM statement) and RQ4 (rare CWEs, inter-procedural vulnerabilities).
- How it informs our work [I]: a peer-reviewed (TOSEM) baseline of the field up to March 2024. It mainly shows two things:
  - As of early 2024, head-to-head SAST-vs-LLM evidence was almost absent.
  - Dataset quality, small input granularity and missing workflow integration were already named as key gaps.

  Its LLM-vs-SAST statement should be cited to the primary study `zhou2024comparison`, not to this survey.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | Only one study in the 58-study corpus compares LLMs with SAST tools (repo level). It reports that SAST tools have low detection rates with few false positives, while LLMs detect more but with high false-positive rates. Second-hand, and the study is the survey authors' own | 18, 22 | A | weak |
| RQ2 | Most LLM detection studies work at function level (7 at line level, 0 at class level, 1 at repo level) | 17–18 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Detection datasets mostly use heuristic labels from vulnerability-fixing commits, which prior work has shown to be noisy | 18 | A | moderate |
| RQ2 | Benchmarks may overlap with LLM pre-training corpora (data contamination); contamination-free benchmarks are recommended | 20 | A | moderate |
| RQ4 | LLMs reportedly struggle more with less frequent CWE types and with inter-procedural and multi-unit vulnerabilities | 20 | A | weak |
| RQ5 | Building a high-quality vulnerability detection benchmark remains an open challenge; a curated, living, manually verified test set is proposed | 19, 22 | A | moderate |
| RQ5 | None of the 58 studies is integrated into developer workflows, and almost none supports developer interaction or explanations | 19 | V | moderate |
| RQ5 | Directions still under-explored as of Mar 2024: repo-level detection, LLM agents, external tool use, LLMs customised for vulnerabilities | 22–23 | A | moderate |

## 14. Key quotes
> "Constructing a high-quality vulnerability detection benchmark remains an open challenge to date." (p. 19)

> "all studies in our review are not integrated into developers’ workflows and tools but are evaluated only offline using static and historical data" (p. 19)

> "SAST tools achieve low vulnerability detection rates with relatively low false positives, whereas LLMs can detect more vulnerabilities but tend to suffer from high false positive rates" (p. 22)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: all 24 body pages read (abstract to conclusion, Tables 1–3, Figs. 1–8). The reference list (p. 24–30) was consulted for refs [8], [56], [84] and [128]–[130]. Figures 2–8 are partly garbled in the text layer, so counts were taken from the running text where both exist.
- Version: arXiv v3 (Oct 2024). The published TOSEM version (DOI 10.1145/3708522) was not compared.
- Uncertainties:
  - The denominators of the 73/17/10% technique shares are not stated.
  - The abstract's split of 43 published + 15 preprints is not reconciled with the 37 + 5 papers after QA plus 16 snowballed papers.
- Funding / conflict of interest: funded by the National Research Foundation, Singapore (p. 24). The only SAST-vs-LLM evidence in the survey is the authors' own work ([130]).
